entries.title: What is an algorithm?
entries.answer: An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or doing a job. Imagine looking for your name in a list that is sorted from A to Z. One plan is to start at the top and read each name in order. Another is to start near the middle and decide which half to keep looking in. Both can find your name, but the second plan can save time on a long sorted list. Computers can follow algorithms when each step is clear enough for them to carry it out.

sections.heading: A useful rule can have a condition
sections.text: If the name at the middle comes before yours, look in the later half. If it comes after yours, look in the earlier half.

facts: An algorithm can be followed by a person as well as by a computer.
Fast ways of looking through a sorted list depend on the list being in order.

entries.title: Why do computers use 0s and 1s?
entries.answer: A computer can store a tiny piece of information in one of two states. We give those states the names 0 and 1. One such choice is called a bit. Put bits together and you can make patterns. A set of agreed rules can tell a computer which pattern stands for a letter, a number, or a color. Binary numbers use only 0 and 1. Their places count in ones, twos, fours, eights, and so on, each place worth twice as much as the one to its right.

sections.heading: Read 101 in binary
sections.text: Start at the right. There is one 1, no 2s, and one 4. Add them together and you get 5.

facts: Three bits can make eight different patterns.
